newsitem.title: UK: Weaker dollar reverses stock, bond rises.
newsitem.headline: Weaker dollar reverses stock, bond rises.

text.p: A sharp drop in the U.S. dollar overnight pressured European stocks and bonds at the start of European trading on Thursday.

The dollar tumbled overnight after Japanese finance ministry official Eisuke Sakakibara said the dollar's recovery from last year's global post-war low against the yen was nearly complete and Japan's economy was stronger than markets believed.

Those comments started a dollar slide, sparking a sell-off in Japanese stocks and bonds as fears emerged that foreign investors would start pulling money out of Japan if the dollar were to take another lengthy trip southward. That would devalue their Japanese holdings.

"A continued yen weakening would have encouraged the outlook on Japanese corporate earnings, but such a rise hurts the prospects of foreign investor buying," said Tetsuya Ishijima, chief strategist at Okasan Securities Co Ltd in Tokyo.
Japanese stocks and bonds were also spooked by ideas of a stronger-than-expected Japanese economy that could ignite inflation and lead to higher interest rates there.

"The initial signal did not come from the new U.S. administration as many expected but from Japan, where it appears the groundwork is being laid for a rate hike," said Klaus Baader, senior currency economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
The Nikkei-225 closed down 220.41 index points, or 1.05 percent, at 20,771.11.
In early London, the dollar dipped below 112 yen, giving up some of its 40-percent gain since its record low last year.
By 1030 GMT the dollar was at 1.5086 marks and 111.83 yen, compared with 1.5165 marks and 113.83 yen in late European trade on Tuesday.
The overall weakness in Japan overshadowed Wall Street's 97-point surge in the Dow Industrials index to a record close on Wednesday of 6,178 points and dampened European stocks.
"We had a celebratory mark-up on Wall Street but I don't think it is likely to keep going," a senior equities dealer said about the blue chip FTSE 100 stock index in London.
Quick rounds of profit-taking and general fears of higher interest rates, reflected in weaker government bond prices throughout Europe, kept a lid on European bourses.

The FTSE opened higher but immediately slipped into negative ground, with inflation and interest rate worries lingering from Wednesday's central bank report. On Wednesday, the Bank of England forecast an imminent rise in inflation and the probable need for higher interest rates.
French blue-chips eased about 0.80 percent as investors sold some stock to lock in profits after the CAC-40 jumped to its highest level since 1994 in post-U.S. elections euphoria on Wednesday.
German shares slid in-line with the dollar and weak corporate results. Siemens fell sharply after it forecast flat output for 1996-7 and Daimler-Benz AG was down after reporting nine-month resuts.
CURRENCIES AT 1030 GMT
The dollar was at 1.5086 marks and 111.83 yen, compared with 1.5165 marks and 113.83 yen in late European trade on Tuesday.
STOCK MARKETS AT 1030 GMT
LONDON - The Financial Times-Stock Exchange index of 100 leading British shares was 25.2 points lower at 3,910.5.
PARIS - The CAC-40 share index was down 17.70 at 2,195.67
FRANKFURT - The 30-share DAX index fell 13.40 at 2,715.79.
PRECIOUS METALS AT 1030 GMT
Gold fixed at $377.90 against $378.00 previously after it eased overnight on selling in Tokyo and Australian producer sales. Silver was down three cents at $4.75.
